author: Claude (EFL materials writer role)
basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.

slides.1: Taiwan's high-tech system looks wonderful on paper, but has it really reached everybody? For the next six minutes I want to hold online learning up to the light and look.
slides.2: The fourth goal has always been about fair education for everyone. It should not matter where on the map you were born. Taiwan lives on advanced technology, yet we hardly teach the responsible side of it.
slides.3: We have spent a fortune on classroom technology, because that high-tech industry pays our national bills. The birth rate is now at a record low. The tools change every year, so our priorities need a rethink.
slides.4: The divide starts with the connection itself. A city student streams a lesson without thinking, while a school in the mountains waits for a page to load. The gap grows every time the curriculum moves online.
slides.5: Information arrives faster than anyone can check it. Most of us scroll through social media for hours, yet almost nobody has been taught how to test a story. Our judgement weakens without us noticing.
slides.6: Safety online has become a crisis, not a side issue. Cyberbullying and harassment keep climbing, and the damage lands on a student's mental health. If schools will not act, who exactly is protecting them?
slides.7: Now the achievements, because there are real ones. The government's "tablets for every student" policy has handed devices to thousands of rural children. Owning a screen and learning from it are not the same thing.
slides.8: Public platforms are the quieter success story. Free courses have been put online by the government. A disadvantaged family can now learn coding at the kitchen table, and that quietly narrows the class gap.
slides.9: Our schools sit above the world average for how many students take part. Teachers have been given serious training in distance teaching. But a laptop in every hand can hide how shallow a lesson becomes.
slides.10: The good news is that media literacy has entered the curriculum. Pupils now practice checking a source before they pass it on. Most adults in this room never had a similar opportunity at school.
slides.11: More than 80% of our schools have taken up digital tools. Some now run AI assistants that set each student different homework. Those chips come from our factories, though nobody teaches the ethics.
slides.12: Some of the answers have to travel by road. Vans fitted out as digital classrooms now drive into the mountain villages. They carry robotics kits and coding workshops to the children who would never meet them.
slides.13: Why should any of this matter to you? Because those digital skills sit underneath exports worth about 500 billion US dollars every year. The identical skills will be needed for data science and climate technology.
slides.14: There is a real price for this screen time. Internet addiction is growing among teenagers, and sleep, energy and family life usually go first. If nothing changes, that damage will follow them into adult years.
slides.15: If we let these digital gaps harden, a generation of ability will simply be wasted. We are the college students in this room. So we should be asking whether regulation moves as fast as automation.
slides.16: A society that can read the internet well is much harder to fool. Without steady reform, Taiwan will slip behind in digital innovation. Media literacy has to grow up with the technology it explains.
slides.17: So where exactly has that left us? Taiwan has built one of the best-connected school systems in the world, and that is real progress. But a fast connection has never guaranteed a fair education for everyone.
slides.18: We should challenge the comfortable story. Device numbers are impressive and test scores look fine, yet a screen is watched for hours without a single original thought. Deep reform has to start exactly there.
slides.19: In the years ahead, digital rights have to include the groups that usually get left out. The curriculum needs a proper update. Every course should connect its content to the internet students actually use.
slides.20: Here is the ask. Join a policy discussion, volunteer for a media literacy class, or simply show a younger student how to check a source. That digital future depends on people like us.
